claims.text: Adding approximately 3 wt% Cu to a tungsten-based HEA intermediate layer will produce finely dispersed, coherent Cu nanoprecipitates.
The Cu addition will improve heat-transfer capability without degrading structural integrity.
Conventional tungsten-based HEAs used for this application typically have dendritic or equiaxed microstructures and are mechanically robust.
Introducing Cu during alloy synthesis will promote in situ precipitation of coherent Cu nanoparticles in the HEA matrix.
Temperatures of 400–600 °C and moderate mechanical loading are representative service conditions for intermediate layers in plasma-facing components.
Finely dispersed coherent Cu nanoprecipitates will create enhanced electron-conduction pathways through the HEA matrix.
Copper has high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
At a minor concentration, Cu nanoprecipitates will connect across the disordered matrix to form a heat-conduction network dominated by electronic transport.
Coherent precipitate interfaces can relieve stress concentrations associated with premature crack initiation and thereby support strength and ductility.
Coherent Cu precipitates specifically will avoid cracks or stress concentrators and preserve the mechanical strength of the Cu-modified HEA.
The Cu-modified HEA will have 10–20% higher effective thermal conductivity than the Cu-free baseline.
The Cu-modified HEA will preserve baseline yield strength and ductility at 400–600 °C under reactor-relevant mechanical loading.
The current Cu-free tungsten-based HEA intermediate layer meets structural requirements.
The baseline HEA has limited heat-transfer capability because high matrix disorder causes phonon scattering.
The beneficial effect will occur only below approximately 3–5 wt% Cu.
Excessive Cu may cause phase segregation or embrittlement.
Cu contents substantially below the proposed range may not produce a measurable thermal-conductivity improvement.
Tungsten is a candidate plasma-facing material because of properties including high melting point, thermal conductivity, and thermomechanical stability.
Laser-cladded WTaVTiZr high-entropy alloys can have a single BCC phase, dendritic morphology, and microstructural stability after annealing at 900 °C for 5–10 h.
The exact conductivity gain, mechanical-property trade-off, and optimal Cu concentration remain uncertain pending experimental validation.
